publisher: Ba, Kiros, Hinton · University of Toronto
title: Layer Normalization: averaging across neurons instead of batches made it a Transformer staple
summary: Batch normalization computes means and variances across a batch of samples, so it struggles with small batches and is hard to apply to RNNs. Layer normalization computes them across the neurons of one layer for a single sample, making it independent of the batch. We work through the difference by hand, examine its invariance properties, RNN results, and weaknesses on convolutional networks, then look at how it was adapted twice inside the Transformer.
ai_summary: In “Layer Normalization” (Ba, Kiros, Hinton, University of Toronto, 2016), batch normalization’s “compute statistics across a batch of samples” becomes “compute the mean and variance across all neurons in the same layer for a single sample,” followed by a learned gain and bias. It does not depend on batch size, uses the same computation at training and test time, and can be computed separately at each time step of an RNN. The paper analyzes its invariance to scaling and shifting the entire weight matrix and to scaling a single sample, and shows faster training on image-caption retrieval, reading comprehension, sentence representation, DRAW, and handwriting generation; on convolutional networks, it is not as good as batch normalization.
brief: Problem: batch normalization depends on batch size, behaves differently at training and test time, and is hard to use on RNNs with variable-length sequences.
Method: compute the mean and variance across all neurons in the same layer for a single sample, normalize, then apply a learned gain and bias.
Result: independent of batch size and usable at every time step; RNN tasks generally train faster, with better results on image-caption retrieval, sentence representation, and more.
Limitation: not as good as batch normalization on convolutional networks; later moved to the input of each sublayer in Transformers and simplified to RMSNorm.

cover.headline: A close reading of the Layer Normalization paper
cover.highlight: Normalizes each sample independently of the batch

nodes.label: Subtract mean, divide by standard deviation

sections.h: The short version: what the paper actually does

blocks.p: In July 2016, Jimmy Lei Ba, Jamie Ryan Kiros, and Geoffrey Hinton at the University of Toronto published this paper. The first author was also one of the authors of “Adam.”

It aims to improve **batch normalization**, which Google introduced a year earlier. Batch normalization takes each neuron, looks at its inputs across the current batch of training samples, computes the mean and variance, and “standardizes” the inputs to mean 0, variance 1. It made feedforward networks train much faster, but it has two hard problems: it depends on batch size and fails when the batch is too small, and it is hard to use in recurrent neural networks (RNNs), because every time step would need its own statistics.

Layer normalization changes only the direction of averaging: **instead of computing statistics across samples in a batch, it computes them across all neurons in the same layer for the same sample**. Each sample normalizes itself, so it does not matter who else is in the batch or how large the batch is. Training and test computations are exactly the same. In an RNN, you only need to compute the statistics once at each time step.

The paper evaluates six kinds of tasks, with the focus on RNNs: image-caption retrieval, reading comprehension, sentence representation, image generation, handwriting generation, and MNIST classification. Layer normalization generally trains faster and often gives better results; on convolutional networks, though, it is not as good as batch normalization.

At the time, the paper was aimed mainly at RNNs. What later made it a foundational component was the Transformer: from the original 2017 Transformer to GPT-2 and LLaMA, nearly every layer relies on layer normalization or a simplified version.

callout.title: The one-sentence version
callout.text: Batch normalization: take one neuron and compute the mean and variance across a batch of samples. Layer normalization: take one sample and compute the mean and variance across all neurons in a layer. Change the direction, and you are no longer dependent on the batch.

callout.title: Three small concepts you need for this paper
callout.text: Don’t worry if they are unfamiliar; these three are enough:
list: **A neuron’s input (summed input)**: the previous layer’s outputs multiplied by the weights and summed, written a. This is what gets normalized, before the bias and activation function are applied.
**Standardization**: subtract the mean and divide by the standard deviation, so that a set of numbers has mean 0 and standard deviation 1.
**Recurrent neural network (RNN)**: at each time step, it processes one word with the same set of weights and passes the hidden state to the next step. See the Seq2Seq close reading for more.

sections.h: Background: what batch normalization gets right, and where it gets stuck

blocks.p: The paper first lays out the problem: in a deep network, the gradient for one layer’s weights depends heavily on the previous layer’s neuron outputs. If those outputs change in a highly correlated way, the next layer must constantly adapt. The batch normalization paper called this “covariate shift,” and the fix is to standardize each neuron’s summed input:

parts.desc: The input to the i-th neuron
The mean and standard deviation of this neuron’s input over the entire training data
A learnable gain, applied after standardization to restore a useful scale

formula.note: Computing the expectation over the whole dataset is too expensive, so in practice it is estimated from the current mini-batch. The paper notes that this constrains the batch size and makes batch normalization hard to apply to RNNs.

plain.title: Batch normalization needs the whole class before it can rank you
plain.text: Batch normalization is like ranking by subject across the whole class: for a single neuron, you need that neuron’s value on every sample in the batch to compute the average and spread. If only one student shows up (batch size 1), there is no ranking; at test time, you have to make do with the historical average from training.

list: **Depends on batch size**: with a small batch, the mean and variance estimates are very unreliable; with batch size 1, they cannot be computed at all. This rules out online learning, and also distributed training where each device can hold only a very small batch.
**Training and test time differ**: during training you use the current batch’s statistics, but at test time you must use a moving average accumulated during training.

**Awkward for RNNs**: sequences have different lengths. The obvious application would require storing a separate set of statistics for each time step, and a test sequence longer than any training sequence would have no statistics to use.

blocks.p: Batch normalization has a side benefit: because every batch is different, the noisy statistics act as a regularizer. Layer normalization gives that up.

sections.h: Layer normalization: averaging in a different direction

blocks.p: The paper’s observation is that changes in one layer’s outputs tend to change all of the next layer’s summed inputs together, in a correlated way—especially with activations such as ReLU, whose outputs can change a lot. So the authors propose fixing the mean and variance of the summed inputs within each layer:

parts.desc: Number of neurons in this layer
The mean and standard deviation across all neurons in this layer for the same sample. All neurons in the layer share this pair, but each sample gets its own.
A gain and bias for each neuron, applied after normalization and before the activation function, so the network can still express any scale and offset.

formula.note: The only difference from batch normalization is the direction of the average. The paper emphasizes that layer normalization imposes no constraint on batch size and works even for pure online learning with batch size 1.

plain.title: A different direction of averaging
plain.text: Lay out a batch as a table: rows are samples, columns are neurons. Batch normalization computes down the columns (blue; one column across all samples), and layer normalization computes across the rows (green; one row across all neurons). Computing across a row only needs that single sample, so it does not matter which other samples are in the batch, or how many there are.

fig.title: Worked example: the same batch gives completely different results under the two normalization methods
fig.subtitle: Illustrative: a layer with 4 neurons and a batch of 3 samples. The numbers are made up for this article; sample 3 is exactly 10× sample 1. Standard deviations use the population formula.
fig.note: Under layer normalization, sample 1 and the 10× larger sample 3 produce exactly the same result; the pattern of which neurons are larger or smaller within each sample is preserved. Under batch normalization, sample 1’s result depends on which other samples are in the batch: change the batch, and its output shifts from about −0.6 to 1.

callout.title: Two normalization methods, two ways of grading
callout.text: Batch normalization is like ranking by subject: in math, you look at your position in the class. Layer normalization is like checking how lopsided your own grades are: line up all your subjects and see which are relatively strong and weak. The first needs the whole class’s scores; the second only needs your own report card.

quiz.q: Why does batch normalization fail at batch size 1 while layer normalization still works?
options: Layer normalization does not need to compute a standard deviation.

Batch normalization computes variance across samples in the batch; with one sample the variance is 0. Layer normalization computes across all neurons of the same sample, so it is independent of batch size
Layer normalization is only used at test time.
quiz.why: Batch normalization computes statistics for each neuron across samples, so with one sample the variance is 0 and there is nothing to divide by. Layer normalization computes statistics for each sample across neurons, so it works as long as the layer has more than one neuron.

sections.h: Using layer normalization in RNNs: compute once at each time step

blocks.p: At each step, an RNN’s input is formed from the previous hidden state and the current input: a_{t} = W_{hh} · h_{t−1} + W_{xh} · x_{t}. Layer normalization applies directly:

parts.desc: Computed from the current step and current layer only, so the sequence length does not matter.
Gain and bias, shared across all time steps.

plain.title: Every step resets the volume to normal
plain.text: As an RNN processes a sequence step by step, the signal tends to keep growing or shrinking. That is exactly the source of exploding and vanishing gradients. Layer normalization pulls all of the current step’s inputs back to “mean 0, variation 1” at every step, like turning the volume back to a standard setting at each stop. The signal never grows too loud or too quiet.

blocks.p: The paper explains why this is especially suited to RNNs: in a standard RNN, the average magnitude of the inputs to a recurrent unit tends to grow or shrink at every step, and that is the source of exploding and vanishing gradients. After layer normalization, scaling all summed inputs of a layer up or down together does not change the output, so the hidden-state dynamics are much more stable.

The supplementary material gives a concrete LSTM recipe: apply layer normalization separately to the “hidden state times weights” and “input times weights” terms before adding them, and apply it once to the memory cell c_{t} before the tanh.

sections.h: Theory: what each of the three normalization methods is insensitive to

blocks.p: The paper puts batch normalization, weight normalization (which divides by the length of the weight vector instead of the variance), and layer normalization into a single framework: in every case, subtract μ, divide by σ, then apply a learned gain and bias. The only difference is how μ and σ are computed. It then compares which transformations each method is “invariant” to—meaning transformations that leave the model output completely unchanged.

fig.title: Invariance properties of the three normalization methods
fig.subtitle: From Table 1 of the paper. “Invariant” means the transformation does not change the model output.
rows: Scale the entire weight matrix by a constant
Shift every row of the weight matrix by the same vector
Scale a single neuron’s incoming weight vector
Scale the entire dataset by a constant
Scale a single sample by a constant
fig.note: The last row is unique to layer normalization: scaling one sample by any factor does not change the prediction. That is why samples 1 and 3 in the worked example above produce the same result.

blocks.p: **Why layer normalization is insensitive to scaling a single sample**: if sample x is multiplied by δ, all inputs to the layer are multiplied by δ, and μ and σ are also multiplied by δ, so (a − μ) / σ is unchanged. Batch normalization cannot do this, because its μ and σ also depend on the other samples in the batch.

plain.title: Scaling everything up, the shape stays the same
plain.text: If all inputs of a sample are multiplied by 10 (red), the mean and spread are also multiplied by 10. After subtracting the mean and dividing by the spread, the resulting shape is exactly the same. That is why layer normalization is insensitive to how large the sample is overall.

blocks.p: The paper also analyzes learning through the geometry of the parameter space (the Fisher information matrix) and reaches two intuitive conclusions:

list: **Longer weights learn more slowly**: after normalization, making a weight vector longer does not change the model output, but σ becomes larger too, so an update of the same absolute size has less effect on the output. In effect, the weight vector’s length automatically lowers its own learning rate. This acts as an implicit early-stopping effect, making training more stable near convergence.

**The gain is easier to learn**: in a normalized model, the “size” of a weight is handled separately by the gain parameter. The paper derives that, when learning the gain, a parameter change affects the output only through the size of the prediction error, not through the input scale as in ordinary models. This makes it more robust to scaling of inputs and parameters.

plain.title: The bigger the steering wheel, the less it turns for the same force
plain.text: After normalization, making the whole weight vector longer does not change the output, but the same-sized update becomes smaller relative to its length. This is equivalent to the learning rate automatically shrinking. The longer the weights, the smaller each update, and training naturally becomes more stable.

blocks.p: Unless noted otherwise, the gain is initialized to 1 and the bias to 0 in the experiments.

fig.note: The paper also trained the layer-normalized model for a month (about 1.7 million iterations), and every task except one (MR) improved further.

blocks.p: **A detail where layer normalization differs from batch normalization.** The authors of recurrent batch normalization found that the gain’s initial value must be chosen carefully; they set it to 0.1. This paper tried initial gain values of 1.0 and 0.1 for layer normalization and found that 1.0 was clearly better, suggesting that layer normalization is not as sensitive to the initial scale as recurrent batch normalization.

**Convolutional networks are the weak spot.** The paper’s preliminary experiments show that layer normalization is faster than no normalization, but batch normalization is better. The explanation: in fully connected layers, neurons contribute roughly equally to the final prediction, so normalizing them together is fine. In convolutional networks, neurons whose receptive fields lie at image edges are rarely active, and their statistics differ sharply from other neurons in the same layer, so forcing them into one average is not appropriate. In the MNIST experiment, the authors also deliberately did not normalize the final softmax layer, because its output scale determines the model’s confidence.

callout.title: “Layer normalization has completely replaced batch normalization”
callout.text: Not really. On convolutional networks and image tasks, batch normalization is still widely used, and the paper itself admits that layer normalization is worse there. Layer normalization became a standard mainly in sequence models such as RNNs and, later, Transformers: variable-length sentences, limited batch sizes, and the need for consistent training and inference are exactly where batch normalization is weak.

list: **The supplementary material swaps the gain and bias.** In equation (15) of the supplementary material, α multiplies the normalized value (the gain) and β is added (the bias). But the text below says α and β "are the additive and multiplicative parameters, respectively," and that α is initialized to 0 and β to 1. If the gain α were really initialized to 0, the layer's output would start out as all zeros. Since Section 6 of the main paper says "gain initialized to 1, bias initialized to 0," the supplementary text appears to have the two reversed.

**"Curvature becomes one half" may be missing a square.** Section 5.2.2 says that when the weight length doubles, σ also doubles, so the curvature along this direction becomes half its original value. But by the paper's own equation (13), the Fisher information block along this direction is proportional to 1 / σ^{2}, so after doubling it should be one quarter. This does not affect the conclusion that longer weights learn more slowly.

**The "covariate shift" explanation was later questioned.** The paper follows the batch normalization paper in saying that normalization works because it reduces "covariate shift." A 2018 study by Santurkar et al. argues that batch normalization mainly smooths the loss landscape and has little to do with covariate shift. Why normalization works is still debated.

**Direct comparisons with batch normalization are limited.** The paper only compares directly against batch normalization on MNIST classification and reading comprehension, where the batch normalization results are cited from other work. For convolutional networks it gives only a qualitative description, no numbers.

sections.h: Afterward: a Transformer staple, and two major changes

blocks.p: A year later, the Transformer put layer normalization into every layer: each sublayer (attention or feedforward network) is wrapped in a residual connection, then layer normalization is applied, giving `LayerNorm(x + Sublayer(x))` (see the Transformer close reading). From then on, it and the residual connection together formed the backbone of the Transformer. It later went through two important changes:

fig.title: How layer normalization's placement changed across the main-line models
fig.subtitle: From the model architecture sections of the respective papers
rows: Moved to each sublayer's input, with one more at the end
fig.note: The GPT-2 paper says this placement is similar to a "pre-activation" residual network. The LLaMA paper says normalization is placed at the input to improve training stability.

list: **Moved to the input (Pre-LN).** The original Transformer adds first, then normalizes; GPT-2 normalizes the sublayer input first, then computes the sublayer, then adds the residual. This leaves the residual "main path" clear of any normalization, so both signal and gradient can pass straight through, making much deeper models easier to train.

**Dropping the mean (RMSNorm).** In 2019, Zhang and Sennrich proposed dividing by the root mean square only, without subtracting the mean; it performs comparably but is cheaper to compute. LLaMA adopted it, and many open-source large models have followed suit since.

plain.title: Before the sublayer or after it?
plain.text: The original Transformer computes the sublayer, adds the input back, then normalizes (Post-LN). Later models, GPT-2 and LLaMA, normalize first, compute the sublayer, then add the input back (Pre-LN). This leaves the residual shortcut—the path that copies the input straight through—with nothing in the way, making models with dozens or hundreds of layers easier to train.

blocks.p: The next article in this line changes direction: the model sees tokens, not characters. **BPE subword tokenization** decides what counts as one token.

sections.h: Check yourself: did you really get it?

quiz.q: If you multiply all the inputs of a single training sample by 10, what happens to the layer-normalized network's prediction for it?
options: The prediction is also multiplied by 10.
It stays the same: the layer's inputs, μ, and σ all scale by 10, so the normalized values are identical.
It depends on the other samples in the batch.
quiz.why: This is layer normalization's unique "single-sample scale invariance" (the last row of Table 1 in the paper). Batch normalization cannot do this, because its statistics also depend on the other samples in the batch.

quiz.q: Why is layer normalization not as good as batch normalization on convolutional networks?
options: Different positions in a convolutional layer have very different statistics—for example, neurons at image edges are rarely activated—so it is inappropriate to average them together.
quiz.why: Layer normalization assumes the neurons in a layer are roughly comparable and can be standardized together. Fully connected layers mostly satisfy this; convolutional layers do not. The paper says this deserves further study.

quiz.q: From the original Transformer to LLaMA, what two changes did layer normalization go through?
options: It switched back from layer normalization to batch normalization.
Its position moved from after the sublayer to the sublayer input, and it was simplified to RMSNorm, which divides only by the root mean square.
It is only used in the last layer.
quiz.why: GPT-2 moved it to the input of every sublayer, and LLaMA further switched to RMSNorm. Both changes were made to make very deep models more stable to train and cheaper to compute.

blocks.p: After reading this, you should be able to answer these questions:

list: In which direction do batch normalization and layer normalization compute their mean and variance?
What are the limitations of batch normalization, and how does layer normalization avoid them?
Why is layer normalization particularly well suited to RNNs?
What are the gain and bias for? Why add them after normalization?
Which transformations is layer normalization invariant to, and which is it not?
Why does making the weights longer automatically lower the learning rate?
How did layer normalization's position in the Transformer change later?
